summary: Sorafenib is an oral multikinase inhibitor used for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma, advanced renal cell carcinoma, and radioactive-iodine-refractory differentiated thyroid carcinoma. It targets both tumor-cell signaling kinases and angiogenic receptor kinases. Characteristic and clinically important toxicities include hand-foot skin reaction and other dermatologic toxicity, hepatotoxicity (including drug-induced hepatitis), hypertension, hemorrhage, QT prolongation, cardiac ischemia/infarction, and GI perforation. It is taken on an empty stomach at 400 mg twice daily and requires careful monitoring with dose interruption/reduction for toxicity.
indications: Locally recurrent or metastatic, progressive, differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC) refractory to radioactive iodine

dosage.d: 400 mg twice daily without food until no longer benefiting or unacceptable toxicity
dosage.n: Take at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal

dosage.d: First reduction 400 mg once daily; then 400 mg every other day
dosage.n: For adverse reactions per label tables

dosage.d: Reduce to 600 mg/day (400 mg + 200 mg 12 h apart), then 400 mg/day, then 200 mg/day

admin: Take on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating
Interrupt, reduce, or discontinue for adverse reactions per labeled dose-modification tables
Withhold for at least 10 days before and after major surgery (wound-healing/hemorrhage risk)
moa: Sorafenib inhibits multiple kinases involved in tumor cell proliferation and angiogenesis. It blocks intracellular serine/threonine kinases (CRAF, wild-type and mutant BRAF) in the RAF/MEK/ERK pathway and receptor tyrosine kinases including VEGFR-1, VEGFR-2, VEGFR-3, PDGFR-beta, c-KIT, FLT-3 and RET. Inhibition of the VEGF and PDGF receptors suppresses tumor angiogenesis while RAF kinase inhibition impairs tumor cell signaling and proliferation.

absolute: Known severe hypersensitivity to sorafenib or any component
Use in combination with carboplatin and paclitaxel in patients with squamous cell lung cancer
relative: Congenital long QT syndrome or uncorrected electrolyte abnormalities
Significant cardiac ischemia or recent myocardial infarction
monitor: ECG/QT interval and serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium)
Skin, bleeding, and signs of GI perforation

preg: Based on its mechanism and animal data, sorafenib can cause fetal harm (teratogenicity, embryo-fetal toxicity). Advise patients of the risk; women of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose, and males with female partners should also use contraception.
lact: Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the breastfed infant, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 2 weeks after the final dose.
renal: No dose adjustment is required for mild to moderate renal impairment. Sorafenib has not been studied in patients on dialysis or with severe renal impairment; use with caution and monitor.
hepatic: Sorafenib can cause drug-induced hepatitis with hepatic failure and death; monitor liver function and discontinue if significant hepatotoxicity occurs (transaminase rise without an alternative cause). No specific dosing recommendation is available for severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment; use with caution. Note it is itself used in hepatocellular carcinoma where baseline liver function is often impaired.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) - reduce sorafenib exposure; avoid
Warfarin/anticoagulants - bleeding risk; monitor INR closely
moderate: Docetaxel, doxorubicin, irinotecan, fluorouracil (altered exposure of co-administered drug)
UGT1A1/UGT1A9 substrates (sorafenib may increase their exposure)
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach; a high-fat meal reduces bioavailability by about 30%.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; minimize in hepatic impairment.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise lipase/amylase, transaminases and bilirubin, lower phosphate, and prolong the QT interval on ECG.

emergency: Acute cardiac event / arrhythmia from QT prolongation

monitoring: Blood pressure weekly for the first 6 weeks then periodically
Liver function tests at baseline and during therapy
Skin examination, bleeding signs, and TSH (especially in DTC)
counsel: Take on an empty stomach, an hour before or two hours after food
Report redness, pain, blistering or peeling of palms and soles early - this hand-foot reaction is common and manageable
Tell your team about unusual bleeding or bruising, severe belly pain, chest pain, or a severe rash
Use effective contraception during and after treatment; do not breastfeed
Keep all blood-pressure and blood-test appointments; tell your dentist/surgeon before any procedure
pk: Steady-state plasma concentrations reached within about 7 days
Median time to peak plasma concentration about 3 hours
Twice-daily dosing maintains exposure; effect continues with ongoing dosing
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep in original container, protect from moisture
pearls: Signature toxicity quartet to remember: hand-foot skin reaction, hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, and hemorrhage
Must be taken on an empty stomach - food cuts absorption substantially
Monitor blood pressure weekly for the first 6 weeks; hypertension is early and common
Strong CYP3A4 inducers reduce efficacy - avoid combinations like rifampin and St John's wort
Hold around major surgery (about 10 days before and after) because of impaired wound healing and bleeding
missed: If a dose is missed, skip it and take the next dose at the usual time; do not take a double dose. Contact the oncology team for guidance.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. The adverse reactions seen at 800 mg twice daily (twice the recommended dose) were mainly diarrhea and dermatologic effects. In suspected overdose, withhold sorafenib and provide supportive care, monitoring liver function, blood pressure, ECG/QT and for bleeding or dermatologic toxicity.
